nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Light drives the island forest, the algae and the reef corals alike.

nodes.name: Rainfall
nodes.desc: Rain on the mountains feeds the forest of the island, which is wetter on its high southern peaks.

nodes.name: East Australian Current
nodes.desc: Warm water carried south by this current lets the most southerly true coral reef grow, and mixes tropical and temperate marine life.

nodes.name: Forest soil
nodes.desc: Soil of the island forest, enriched by leaf litter and the work of decomposers.

nodes.name: Kentia palm
nodes.desc: A palm found naturally only on Lord Howe Island, and a defining tree of its forests. Wild seeds are collected for a regulated export trade.

nodes.name: Yellow tulipwood
nodes.desc: A fruiting native forest tree recorded very often on the island in GBIF data. It is part of the native forest canopy.

nodes.name: Benthic algae
nodes.desc: Over 305 species of seaweed have been recorded in the marine park, about 15 percent of them found nowhere else. They are the grazing base of the reef.

nodes.name: Reef corals
nodes.desc: Reef-building corals form the most southerly true coral reef in the world, in a lagoon on the western side of the island.

nodes.name: Lord Howe cicada
nodes.desc: An insect of the island forest. Cicadas feed on plant sap, and many are prey for birds.

nodes.name: Wood-feeding cockroach
nodes.desc: A native cockroach that chews rotting wood and so helps break down dead timber on the forest floor.

nodes.name: Silvereye
nodes.desc: A small bird eating fruit, nectar and insects. It is one of the most commonly recorded birds on the island.

nodes.name: Long-spined sea urchin
nodes.desc: A large dark urchin that grazes algae on rocky reef. Marine park surveys found it increasing about threefold between 2006 and 2010.

nodes.name: Surgeonfishes
nodes.desc: Reef fishes that mostly graze algae from rock and coral, keeping the reef surface cropped.

nodes.name: Reef crustaceans
nodes.desc: Crabs, shrimps and similar animals living among the algae and coral, an important food for many reef fishes.

nodes.name: Lord Howe woodhen
nodes.desc: A flightless rail that eats worms, crustaceans and fruit, and sometimes shearwater eggs. Near 20 birds in the 1970s, it has recovered strongly after feral animals were removed.

nodes.name: Pied currawong
nodes.desc: An omnivorous bird eating insects, fruit and the eggs and young of other birds. The island has its own vulnerable subspecies.

nodes.name: Goatfishes
nodes.desc: Fish that probe the sand for small animals. Goatfish make up about two-thirds of the diet of wedge-tailed shearwaters.

nodes.name: Wrasses
nodes.desc: A varied family of reef fishes that eat small invertebrates; wrasses are common on coral reefs.

nodes.name: Wedge-tailed shearwater
nodes.desc: A seabird that nests in burrows on Lord Howe and hunts fish, squid and crustaceans at sea, diving to depths of up to 66 m.

nodes.name: Flesh-footed shearwater
nodes.desc: A burrow-nesting seabird. Lord Howe holds about 22,000 breeding pairs, though numbers on the island have been declining.

nodes.name: Yellowtail kingfish
nodes.desc: A fast open-water fish that eats other fish and squid. Visitors can hand-feed kingfish at Ned's Beach.

nodes.name: Galápagos shark
nodes.desc: A reef shark that eats mainly bottom-dwelling bony fishes and octopuses. Numbers rose in the marine park sanctuary zones.

nodes.name: Decomposers
nodes.desc: Fungi, bacteria and litter animals that break down leaves, wood and dead seaweed and return nutrients to the soil.
